{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Arthur conjectures''' refer to a set of [[conjecture]]s proposed by [[James Arthur (mathematician)|James Arthur]] in 1989.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last1=Arthur |first1=James |title=Unipotent automorphic representations: conjectures |journal=Astérisque |issue=171 |pages=13–71 |year=1989 |url=http://www.math.toronto.edu/arthur/pdf/34.pdf |issn=0303-1179 |mr=1021499}}</ref> These conjectures pertain to the properties of [[Automorphic form|automorphic representations]] of [[Reductive group|reductive groups]] over [[Adele ring|adele rings]] and the [[Unitary representations of a star Lie superalgebra|unitary representations]] of reductive groups over local fields.<ref name=":0" /> Arthur’s work, which was motivated by the [[Arthur–Selberg trace formula]], suggests a framework for understanding complex relationships in these areas.<ref name=":1">'''{{Citation |last1=Adams |first1=Jeffrey |title=The Langlands classification and irreducible characters for real reductive groups |volume=104 |year=1992 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T37ryFaTWm4C |series=Progress in Mathematics |location=Boston, MA |publisher=Birkhäuser Boston |isbn=978-0-8176-3634-0 |mr=1162533 |last2=Barbasch |first2=Dan |last3=Vogan |first3=David A.}}'''</ref>

Arthur's conjectures have implications for other mathematical theories, notably implying the [[Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture|generalized Ramanujan conjectures]] for [[Cusp form|cusp forms]] on [[General linear group|general linear groups]]. <ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Citation |last1=Clozel |first1=Laurent |title=Automorphic forms and applications |volume=12 |pages=43–93 |year=2007 |editor1-last=Sarnak |editor1-first=Peter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EYsKo1FrLfIC |series=IAS/Park City Math. Ser. |chapter=Spectral theory of automorphic forms |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EYsKo1FrLfIC&pg=PA43 |location=Providence, R.I. |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |isbn=978-0-8218-2873-1 |editor2-last=Shahidi |editor2-first=Freydoon}}</ref> The Ramanujan conjectures, in turn, are central to the study of automorphic forms, as they predict specific behaviors of certain classes of mathematical functions known as cusp forms.<ref name=":2" />

To better understand the Arthur conjectures, familiarity with automorphic forms and reductive groups is useful, as is knowledge of the trace formula developed by Arthur and [[Atle Selberg]]. These mathematical tools allow for analysis of representations of groups in [[number theory]], [[geometry]], and [[physics]].
